steps.say: Oesophageal cancer comes in two very different diseases that happen to share a tube. Squamous cancer grows in the upper and middle thirds and follows years of smoking and drinking. Adenocarcinoma grows at the bottom end on top of Barrett lining, driven by obesity and long standing reflux. Naming the type correctly decides both the operation and the chemotherapy plan.
steps.tx: **Squamous carcinoma** (flat-cell cancer from smoking and alcohol injury) dominates the upper and middle thirds, while **Barrett adenocarcinoma** (gland-forming cancer from Barrett metaplasia) rises in the lower third and junction with obesity and reflux risk. Mixed features are uncommon, so biopsy histology plus tumour level fixes the diagnosis. Each type carries its own nodal pattern, chemosensitivity and operative approach.

steps.say: Junctional tumours are classified by asking one question, where is the centre of the mass. A centre above the cardia is Siewert type one, a centre straddling the cardia is type two, and a centre below it is type three. Types one and two are removed with the oesophagus, while type three needs the whole stomach taken with an extended gastrectomy.
steps.tx: **Siewert** types I to III locate junctional tumours by epicentre against the **gastric cardia** (valve between gullet and stomach). Type I centres above the cardia in Barrett lining, type II straddles the cardia, and type III centres below it in proximal stomach. Types I and II are resected by **oesophagectomy** (gullet removal with gastric pull-up), while type III needs extended total **gastrectomy** (whole stomach removal with Roux-en-Y join).

steps.say: Big tumours are shrunk before surgery, and the regimen depends on fitness and histology. The CROSS schedule is carboplatin and paclitaxel with 41.4 Gy of radiation, and it is given for both main cancer types. Fit patients with adenocarcinoma may instead receive FLOT chemotherapy around the operation. Restaging scans after treatment decide whether the tumour has become removable.
steps.tx: Locally advanced adenocarcinoma gets **CROSS** chemoradiotherapy (combined drugs plus radiation) with **carboplatin**, **paclitaxel** and **41.4** Gy, or perioperative **FLOT** (four-drug chemotherapy around surgery) in fit patients. Response is reassessed with repeat imaging and endoscopy before resection is booked. Poor responders and progressors are spared a futile major operation.

steps.say: Three classic operations remove the gullet, and they differ in how the new join is placed. The Ivor Lewis is done through the belly and the right chest with the join inside the chest. The McKeown adds a neck cut so the join sits in the neck. The transhiatal route avoids opening the chest entirely, which helps frail lungs but leaves the middle of the dissection blind.
steps.tx: **Ivor Lewis** oesophagectomy (two-phase gullet removal) pairs abdominal and right thoracic phases with an intrathoracic **anastomosis** (surgical join inside the chest). **McKeown** resection adds a cervical anastomosis through the neck, keeping leaks out of the chest. **Transhiatal** surgery avoids thoracotomy (chest opening) in frail patients at the cost of blind mediastinal dissection and weaker nodal clearance.

vis.caption: Oesophagectomy approaches with gastric conduit reconstruction after resection. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Cancer surgery is judged by two numbers found in the pathology report. Fifteen nodes is the minimum harvest that stages the disease honestly, because fewer nodes hide positive ones. Five centimetres of clear gullet above the tumour is the proximal margin to aim for. A positive margin, an R1 resection, is followed by recurrence at the join within months.
steps.tx: A minimum **lymph node harvest** (glands removed for staging) of **15** nodes stages oesophageal cancer accurately, since smaller counts understage the disease. **R0 resection** (microscopically clear margins) with **5 cm** proximal clearance is the operative goal. Intraoperative frozen section checks the doughnuts and margins, and further resection follows a positive result.

steps.say: A leak usually announces itself in the first week with a fast pulse, fever and the patient looking septic. Air crackling under the neck skin points to a cervical leak, while dirty chest drains point to a thoracic one. Small contained leaks are drained and stented, but a black dead conduit has no future and must be taken back to theatre.
steps.tx: **Anastomotic leak** (failed surgical join) presents on days **5 to 7** with tachycardia (fast pulse), sepsis and neck crepitus (crackling air under the skin) or chest soilage. Management means drainage, antibiotics, endoscopic vacuum or covered stent for contained leaks. **Conduit necrosis** (dead gastric tube from lost blood supply) mandates reoperation with diversion and delayed rebuild.

nodes.label: Days 5 to 7: fast pulse, sepsis, crepitus

steps.say: Two more complications are watched for on every post operative round. Milky chest drains mean chyle is leaking, and outputs above 1000 mL a day need the thoracic duct tied off. A husky voice means the recurrent laryngeal nerve has been bruised, with aspiration risk until it recovers. Poor tolerance of jejunal feeds is investigated rather than ignored.
steps.tx: **Chyle leak** (milky lymphatic fluid in chest drains) over **1000 mL** per day needs thoracic duct ligation (tying the leaking lymph channel), while low outputs settle with feeds plus octreotide. Jejunal feeding intolerance and **recurrent laryngeal nerve** palsy (voice box nerve injury) with hoarseness are screened routinely after oesophagectomy, because silent aspiration follows nerve injury.

steps.say: Not every patient is routed to the operating theatre. Cancers of the cervical gullet and patients whose hearts and lungs cannot survive a major resection are given definitive chemoradiotherapy as the complete treatment. Surgery re-enters the picture only as salvage, when disease persists or returns after full dose radiation, and everyone consents knowing the risks are higher.
steps.tx: **Definitive chemoradiotherapy** (full-dose combined treatment without planned surgery) suits cervical oesophageal cancer and unfit patients, curing a minority without resection. **Salvage oesophagectomy** (rescue gullet removal) is reserved for residual or recurrent disease after full-dose radiation. Fibrosis from radiation raises leak, pulmonary and mortality risk, so selection stays strict.
